title: Implement Queue using Stacks
description:
Implement a first-in-first-out (FIFO) queue using only two stacks. The implemented queue should support all standard queue operations (`push`, `peek`, `pop`, and `empty`).

Implement the `MyQueue` class:
- `MyQueue()` initializes an empty queue.
- `void push(int x)` pushes element `x` to the back of the queue.
- `int pop()` removes the element from the front of the queue and returns it.
- `int peek()` returns the element at the front of the queue without removing it.
- `boolean empty()` returns `true` if the queue is empty, and `false` otherwise.

Notes:
- You must use only standard stack operations: push to top, peek/pop from top, size, and isEmpty.
- Follow-up: Can you implement the queue such that each operation has amortized `O(1)` time complexity?
constraints: At most 2000 calls will be made to push, pop, peek, and empty.
All calls to pop and peek are valid (the queue is guaranteed to be non-empty).
hints: Maintain two stacks: an input stack for incoming pushes and an output stack for outgoing pops and peeks.
Only transfer elements from the input stack to the output stack when the output stack becomes empty.
Because each element is pushed onto the input stack once, moved to the output stack at most once, and popped once, every operation runs in amortized O(1) time.

examples.explanation: Push 1 then 2 onto the queue. peek() returns 1 (front), pop() removes and returns 1, and empty() returns false since 2 remains.
After popping 10, the queue becomes empty. Pushing 20 and 30 afterwards maintains FIFO order, so peek() returns 20.

title: Implement Stack using Queues
description:
Implement a last-in-first-out (LIFO) stack using only queues. The implemented stack should support all functions of a normal stack (`push`, `top`, `pop`, and `empty`).

Implement the `MyStack` class:
- `MyStack()` initializes an empty stack.
- `void push(int x)` pushes element `x` to the top of the stack.
- `int pop()` removes the element on the top of the stack and returns it.
- `int top()` returns the element on the top of the stack without removing it.
- `boolean empty()` returns `true` if the stack is empty, and `false` otherwise.

Notes:
- You must use only standard queue operations: push to back, peek/pop from front, size, and isEmpty.
- Follow-up: Can you implement the stack using only one queue?
constraints: At most 1000 calls will be made to push, pop, top, and empty.
All calls to pop and top are valid (the stack is guaranteed to be non-empty).
hints: If you maintain a single queue in LIFO order, pop() and top() are simply O(1) front operations.
When pushing a new element x to the back of a queue of size s, rotate the previous s elements from front to back so x moves to the front.

examples.explanation: Push 1 then 2. top() returns 2 (most recently pushed), pop() removes and returns 2, and empty() returns false because 1 is still in the stack.
After pushing 10, 20, 30 and popping 30 and 20, pushing 40 places 40 on top. Popping 40 then 10 leaves the stack empty.

title: Design Circular Queue
description:
Design your implementation of a circular queue (ring buffer). A circular queue is a linear data structure in which operations follow the FIFO (First In First Out) principle and the last position connects back to the first position to form a circle, allowing freed slots at the front to be reused.

Implement the `MyCircularQueue` class:
- `MyCircularQueue(int k)` initializes the object with a fixed capacity of `k`.
- `boolean enQueue(int value)` inserts an element into the circular queue. Returns `true` if the operation is successful, or `false` if the queue is full.
- `boolean deQueue()` deletes an element from the circular queue. Returns `true` if the operation is successful, or `false` if the queue is empty.
- `int Front()` gets the front item from the queue. If the queue is empty, return `-1`.
- `int Rear()` gets the last item from the queue. If the queue is empty, return `-1`.
- `boolean isEmpty()` checks whether the circular queue is empty.
- `boolean isFull()` checks whether the circular queue is full.

You must solve the problem without using a built-in queue data structure.
constraints: At most 3000 calls will be made to enQueue, deQueue, Front, Rear, isEmpty, and isFull.
hints: Use a fixed-size array of length k together with a head index and a current element count.
Tracking count avoids any ambiguity between the empty and full states when head and tail meet.
The tail index for insertion is (head + count) % k, and the rear element sits at (head + count - 1) % k.

examples.explanation: With capacity 3, enQueue(1), enQueue(2), enQueue(3) succeed while enQueue(4) fails. After deQueue(), one slot frees up so enQueue(4) succeeds and Rear() becomes 4.
Querying Front, Rear, or deQueue on an empty queue returns -1 or false. With k = 1, a single element is both Front and Rear.

title: Design Circular Deque
description:
Design your implementation of a circular double-ended queue (deque) with fixed maximum capacity `k`.

Implement the `MyCircularDeque` class:
- `MyCircularDeque(int k)` initializes the deque with a maximum size of `k`.
- `boolean insertFront(int value)` adds an item at the front of the deque. Returns `true` if successful, or `false` if the deque is full.
- `boolean insertLast(int value)` adds an item at the rear of the deque. Returns `true` if successful, or `false` if the deque is full.
- `boolean deleteFront()` deletes an item from the front of the deque. Returns `true` if successful, or `false` if the deque is empty.
- `boolean deleteLast()` deletes an item from the rear of the deque. Returns `true` if successful, or `false` if the deque is empty.
- `int getFront()` returns the front item from the deque, or `-1` if the deque is empty.
- `int getRear()` returns the last item from the deque, or `-1` if the deque is empty.
- `boolean isEmpty()` returns `true` if the deque is empty, or `false` otherwise.
- `boolean isFull()` returns `true` if the deque is full, or `false` otherwise.

You must solve the problem without using a built-in deque data structure.
constraints: At most 2000 calls will be made to insertFront, insertLast, deleteFront, deleteLast, getFront, getRear, isEmpty, and isFull.
hints: Use a fixed-size circular array of length k with a head pointer and an element count.
To insert at the front, move head backward modulo k: head = (head - 1 + k) % k, then write value to buf[head].
To insert or delete at the rear, only the tail position (head + count) % k and count change—head does not move.

examples.explanation: With k = 3, inserting 1 and 2 at the rear and 3 at the front yields [3, 1, 2]. insertFront(4) fails because the deque is full. After deleteLast(), insertFront(4) succeeds and getFront() returns 4.
Operations on an empty deque return -1 for getters and false for deletes. Inserting at the front and deleting from the rear works symmetrically.

title: Number of Recent Calls
description:
You have a `RecentCounter` class that counts the number of recent requests within a 3000-millisecond sliding window.

Implement the `RecentCounter` class:
- `RecentCounter()` initializes the counter with zero recent requests.
- `int ping(int t)` adds a new request at time `t` (in milliseconds) and returns the number of requests that have happened in the past 3000 milliseconds (including the new request). Specifically, return the number of requests whose timestamps fall in the inclusive range `[t - 3000, t]`.

It is guaranteed that every call to `ping` uses a strictly larger value of `t` than the previous call.
constraints: Each test case calls ping with strictly increasing values of t.
At most 10^4 calls will be made to ping.
hints: Because timestamps arrive in strictly increasing order, once a timestamp falls below t - 3000 it can never be inside any future window.
Store timestamps in a FIFO queue: push t at the back, pop all elements strictly less than t - 3000 from the front, and return the queue size.

examples.explanation: At t = 3100, timestamp 100 is exactly on the inclusive boundary [100, 3100], so 2 calls remain. At t = 3101, 100 expires.

title: Design Hit Counter
description:
Design a hit counter which counts the number of hits received in the past 5 minutes (i.e., the past 300 seconds).

Your system accepts a `timestamp` parameter (in seconds granularity), and you may assume that calls are being made to the system in chronological order (i.e., `timestamp` is monotonically non-decreasing). Several hits may arrive at the same timestamp.

Implement the `HitCounter` class:
- `HitCounter()` initializes the object of the hit counter system.
- `void hit(int timestamp)` records a hit that happened at `timestamp` (in seconds).
- `int getHits(int timestamp)` returns the number of hits in the past 5 minutes from `timestamp` (i.e., strictly greater than `timestamp - 300` and less than or equal to `timestamp`: `(timestamp - 300, timestamp]`).
constraints: All calls are made to the system in chronological order (timestamp is monotonically non-decreasing).
At most 10^4 calls will be made to hit and getHits.
hints: Store pairs of (timestamp, count) in a deque along with a running total so multiple hits at the same second collapse into one entry.
Before returning from getHits(timestamp) (and optionally on hit), pop entries from the front whose timestamp is <= timestamp - 300 and subtract their counts from the running total.
Because there are at most 300 distinct seconds in the active window, the deque uses O(1) bounded space and amortized O(1) time per operation.

examples.explanation: Hits at 1, 2, 3 give 3 hits at t = 4. After a hit at 300, getHits(300) returns 4 (range (0, 300]). At t = 301, timestamp 1 expires (1 <= 301 - 300), leaving 3 hits.
Multiple hits at timestamp 10 all count together and expire simultaneously once getHits(310) is called.

title: Dota2 Senate
description:
In the world of Dota2, there are two parties: the Radiant (`'R'`) and the Dire (`'D'`).

The Dota2 senate consists of senators from both parties arranged in a round-based voting order given by a string `senate`, where `senate[i]` is either `'R'` or `'D'`. In each round, every remaining senator takes their turn in left-to-right order and may exercise one of two rights:
1. **Ban one senator's right**: Permanently remove any one opposing senator's rights for the current and all subsequent rounds.
2. **Announce victory**: If all remaining senators with rights belong to the same party, announce victory and end the game.

Assuming every senator plays optimally to help their party win, predict which party will finally announce victory. Return `"Radiant"` or `"Dire"`.
hints: Greedily, a senator should always ban the next opposing senator who has yet to act in the circular order.
Maintain two FIFO queues—one for Radiant indices and one for Dire indices.
Repeatedly compare the front indices of both queues: the senator with the smaller index bans the other and re-enters their queue with index + n for the next round.

examples.explanation: Round 1: The first senator (R) bans the second senator (D). Round 2: Only R remains and announces Radiant victory.
Round 1: R at index 0 bans D at index 1; D at index 2 bans R at index 0. Round 2: Only D at index 2 remains and announces Dire victory.
The two initial Dire senators ban the first two Radiant senators; the last Radiant senator bans one Dire senator, and in round 2 the remaining Dire senator bans the last Radiant senator.

title: Jump Game VI
description:
You are given a 0-indexed integer array `nums` and an integer `k`.

You are initially standing at index `0`. In one move, you can jump at most `k` steps forward without going outside the boundaries of the array. That is, from index `i`, you can jump to any index in the range `[i + 1, min(n - 1, i + k)]` inclusive.

You want to reach the last index of the array (index `n - 1`). Your score is the sum of `nums[j]` for every index `j` you visit along the path (including indices `0` and `n - 1`).

Return the maximum score you can get.
hints: Let dp[i] be the maximum score to reach index i. Then dp[i] = nums[i] + max(dp[j] for i - k <= j < i).
A naive DP transition takes O(k) per index, giving O(nk) time—too slow when both n and k are large.
Maintain a monotonic decreasing deque of (index, dp[index]) pairs over the sliding window [i - k, i - 1] so the maximum is always at the front in O(1) amortized time.

examples.explanation: Choose the path 1 -> -1 -> 4 -> 3 (indices 0, 1, 3, 5) for a total score of 7.
Choose the path 10 -> 4 -> 3 (indices 0, 3, 5) for a total score of 17.
Choose the path 1 -> -5 -> 4 -> 3 -> -3 (indices 0, 1, 3, 5, 7) for a total score of 0.

title: Reveal Cards In Increasing Order
description:
You are given an integer array `deck` where every card has a unique integer value. You may order the deck in any order you want. Initially, all cards start face down in one deck.

You will repeatedly perform the following steps until all cards are revealed:
1. Take the top card of the deck, reveal it, and remove it from the deck.
2. If there are still cards in the deck, move the next top card to the bottom of the deck.
3. Repeat from step 1 while unrevealed cards remain.

Return an ordering of the deck that reveals the cards in strictly increasing order. Note that the first entry in the returned array is considered the top of the deck.
constraints: All values of deck are unique.
hints: Simulate the reveal process on a deque of slot indices [0, 1, ..., n - 1] instead of on the cards themselves.
Sort the deck in ascending order: each time an index is popped from the front of the deque, assign the next smallest card to that index, then move the new front index to the back.

examples.explanation: Starting with [2,13,3,11,5,17,7]: reveal 2 (move 13 to back), reveal 3 (move 11 to back), reveal 5 (move 17 to back), reveal 7 (move 13 to back), reveal 11 (move 17 to back), reveal 13, reveal 17.
With 2 cards, revealing 1 then moving 1000 to the bottom reveals [1, 1000] in increasing order.

title: Logger Rate Limiter
description:
Design a logger system that receives a stream of messages along with their timestamps. Each unique message should only be printed at most once every 10 seconds—that is, a message printed at timestamp `t` prevents any identical message from being printed until timestamp `t + 10` (inclusive).

All messages arrive in chronological order (timestamps are monotonically non-decreasing). Several messages may arrive at the same timestamp.

Implement the `Logger` class:
- `Logger()` initializes the logger object.
- `boolean shouldPrintMessage(int timestamp, String message)` returns `true` if `message` should be printed at `timestamp`, otherwise returns `false`. Note that a rejected (`false`) call does not extend the 10-second cooldown.
constraints: Every timestamp is passed in non-decreasing (chronological) order.
At most 10^4 calls will be made to shouldPrintMessage.
hints: A hash map storing each message's next allowed timestamp works in O(1) time, but keeps expired messages in memory forever.
To bound memory to only the last 10 seconds, pair a FIFO queue of (timestamp, message) entries with a hash set of active messages.
On each call, evict all queue entries with timestamp <= currentTimestamp - 10 from both the queue and the set before checking membership.
spaceComplexity: O(W) where W is unique messages printed in the last 10s

examples.explanation: foo prints at t=1 (blocked until t=11); bar prints at t=2 (blocked until t=12). foo at t=3 and t=10 and bar at t=8 are rejected. At t=11, foo is allowed again.
A message printed at t=0 is rejected at t=9, and allowed again at exactly t=10.
